tagline.text: Ilocos Norte's signature February festival honoring Laoag's patron saint, St. William

location.label: Location
location.text: Laoag City, Ilocos Norte (around Aurora Park, the Provincial Capitol and downtown streets)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Early February to the 10th (feast of St. William); events sometimes run all month

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 days (two days around the feast day cover the main events)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱4,000–10,000 (one night in Laoag, meals and local transport; Manila round trip not included)

children.text: The Pamulinawen Festival is Ilocos Norte's signature festival, centered on February 10, the feast day of Laoag's patron saint, St. William. Floral float parades, street dancing, a calesa procession and Ilocano food feasts fill the downtown streets.

The Pamulinawen Festival takes place every February in Laoag, the capital of Ilocos Norte. It began as a feast-day celebration honoring the city's patron saint, St. William the Hermit. His feast day falls on
February 10

, which has long been observed as Laoag City Day. Over time the religious observance grew into a large festival showcasing the city's culture and heritage. Some sources describe the program as centered on the first week, while the city's tourism information presents the whole of February as festival season, so the length varies slightly from year to year.

The festival takes its name from the Ilocano folk song "Pamulinawen." It is a courting song addressed to a woman of that name who is firm of heart and not easily won, and it is one of the best-loved songs among Ilocanos. The lyrics are known to plead for steadfast love toward someone with a "heart of stone," and the festival borrowed this symbolism to give the St. William feast celebrations a new name. During the festival the song is heard all over the streets.

For visitors, the biggest draw is the street dancing competition, in which teams from each barangay (village) dance out Ilocano traditions and legends. Beyond that, there is the grand float parade, in which large floats decorated with flowers and ornaments roll through downtown; a procession honoring the calesa, the horse-drawn carriage, together with an evening illuminated tour; the Dulang Food Festival, which lays out Ilocano dishes on long communal tables; a beauty pageant; and dance and literary contests. In 2026, Tuesday,
February 10

was declared a special non-working day in Laoag City (Proclamation No. 1154) so that all residents could join the celebration. That same year, Laoag's team also reclaimed the title after 12 years at the 13th Tan-ok ni Ilocano (Festival of Festivals), held on
February 28

The festival is centered on downtown Laoag, especially around Aurora Park and the Ilocos Norte Provincial Capitol. The street dancing procession is known to run along Rizal Street toward the Capitol. Because Laoag is the gateway to the Ilocos region, it is easy to combine the festival with northern sights such as Paoay Church, the La Paz Sand Dunes and the Bangui Windmills. Detailed schedules and venues change slightly each year, so be sure to check announcements from Laoag City Hall and Ilocos Norte tourism before you leave. For first-timers, I recommend two days around the feast day. On the first day, stroll through town at a relaxed pace to get a feel for the park and Capitol area, the market stalls and the calesa stands, then claim a good spot for the parade and street dancing on the second day. Philippine festivals often start later than scheduled, so leave plenty of slack in your plans and bring snacks and drinks to avoid running out of energy. Many local families come out to watch, so the mood is generally relaxed and friendly, and foreigners with cameras are usually welcome.

The centerpiece of the festival. Teams from the city's barangays perform Ilocano history and legends in colorful costumes to the beat of drums. The procession is known to run along the main downtown road toward the Capitol. You also get to enjoy the energy of the crowds lining both sides of the street. The costumes and props are prepared by each village for months, so the care put into the decorations is even clearer up close.

Large floats decorated with flowers and ornaments pass through downtown in a parade themed around Ilocano culture. It is the festival's signature scene, covered by regional television again in 2026. Each float has its own theme and decoration, making it great for photos.

Horse-drawn calesas still run in Laoag's streets today. During the festival there is a procession honoring the calesa and an evening tour with lights, and an orientation event for the drivers (kutseros) is also said to be held. The quiet evening streets give you a taste of the old city.

"Dulang" means table in Ilocano, and the event lays out Ilocano food on long communal tables. It is held near Aurora Park, and you can try signature Ilocos dishes such as bagnet, pinakbet, empanada and longganisa. In 2018, a boodle fight (a communal meal eaten by hand) stretching several kilometers along the city's main avenues was even held as the festival's closing event.

The festival began as the feast of the patron saint, St. William, so religious processions and Mass are held as well. Schedules and venues change from year to year, so check announcements from City Hall and the church. Knowing that the festival began in faith makes the events feel more meaningful.

blocks.title: Cultural shows and market at Aurora Park

children.text: In the evening, cultural shows and concerts are held around Aurora Park, and a festival market selling local crafts, woven goods and snacks is said to be set up. Ilocos garlic, bagnet and woven goods make good souvenirs.

blocks.title: Tan-ok ni Ilocano, the festival of festivals

children.text: Festival teams from several cities in the Ilocos region compete in this event. The 13th edition in 2026 was held on
February 28
, with 22 contingents taking part, and Laoag's team was reported to have won. It gives a sense of how high the standard of the Pamulinawen performances is.

items.title: One-day plan for the feast day
items.subtitle: Centered on the feast of St. William (February 10)

children.text: Arrive in downtown Laoag, leave your bags at your hotel and have breakfast. Roads in the event zone may be closed, so it is best to move around early.
Walk around Aurora Park and the Capitol area to soak up the festival atmosphere, and check the day's official program on City Hall postings or with local information staff.
Try Ilocano food such as bagnet, pinakbet and empanada at the Dulang Food Festival or a downtown restaurant.
Find a spot along the road where the parade and street dancing procession pass, and watch. Start times differ each year, so check on-site announcements.
In the evening, stroll through the shows and market at Aurora Park and, if it is running, take the evening calesa tour.
In some years the feast day is declared a special non-working day, and the city can get very crowded. Book your accommodation in advance.

items.title: Two-night, three-day plan
items.subtitle: The festival and sights of northern Ilocos

children.text: Arrive in Laoag and enjoy the festival events downtown, the evening calesa tour and an Ilocano dinner.
Watch the street dancing and parade in the morning, then enjoy the Dulang Food Festival and the park shows in the afternoon.
Rent a vehicle and stop at the La Paz Sand Dunes or Paoay Church, then return to Laoag and move on.
Public transport is infrequent in northern Ilocos, so it is best not to pack too many places into one day.
A nonstop flight from Manila (MNL) to Laoag International Airport (LAO) takes about
1 hour 15–20 minutes
. Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific are confirmed to fly the route, but schedules vary by season, so check with the airline.
Fares vary greatly by season; some booking sites show prices from
, but they may be higher during the festival.
From the airport, take a tricycle or shared jeepney into town.
Flights sell out quickly during the festival, so book early.
Buses such as Partas, Fariñas, Florida and Genesis run from Manila (PITx and Cubao) to Laoag.
The trip takes about
8–12 hours
depending on the operator and source, and overnight departures arrive at dawn.
Fares are listed from about
for Deluxe to about
for Partas, but check the latest fares with the operator.
You can get around downtown Laoag by tricycle and calesa, and the Aurora Park and Capitol area can be explored on foot.
For sights outside the city, a rental car or a chartered vehicle for the day is the easiest option.
On parade days roads are closed, so walk when you are close to the event zone.
The festival is centered on the feast of St. William on
February 10
, but in some years events begin in the first week of February and run for nearly a month. The detailed program changes every year, so check the latest announcements.
February is the dry season in the Ilocos region, so rain is rarely a concern. The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and sunscreen.

Staying in the downtown area within walking distance of Aurora Park and the Capitol makes it easy to get to the event zone. Rooms fill up quickly during the festival, so book several weeks ahead.

The food is mainly Ilocos cuisine. Be sure to try bagnet (crispy fried pork), pinakbet (vegetables stewed with shrimp paste), Ilocos empanada and longganisa. Among long-established restaurants, La Preciosa is known for Ilocos empanada and Ilocano dishes.
Event start times and road closures change every year, so check City Hall announcements or ask hotel staff right after you arrive.
There is little shade along the street dancing route, so bring a hat, sunglasses and water.
If you want a good spot, head out one or two hours before the event starts.
Event-day movement is heavy, so book your accommodation close to downtown.
A word or two of Ilocano (for example "Agyamanak," thank you) goes over well.
Ilocos garlic, bagnet and woven goods make good souvenirs at the market or the festival stalls.
Do not add far-away places to a festival day; set aside a separate day for the northern sights.
Check the official festival program through City Hall announcements and local news reports, and ask nearby residents about any on-site time changes.

Event schedules, venues and road closures change every year and the official program is sometimes announced late, so be sure to check the latest Laoag City Hall announcements before fixing your travel dates.
The event zone is crowded, so watch out for pickpockets and keep valuables in front of you.
Flights, buses and rooms sell out quickly during the festival.
The midday sun is strong, so watch out for dehydration and heatstroke.
Roads in the event zone are closed and travel slows down, so allow plenty of time.
Choose food with an eye on hygiene.
